standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Spot & remix gender stereotypes in media (UNESCO 3.1, 3.2, 1.3, 2.1-2.3, 5.4). New v2 build, Chapter 3 (matter-of-fact, near-peer). Strategy §7 names this a flagship of the strike & rewrite (UN/RE) signature mechanic. Builds on g10; prereq g16.
evidenceBase: Gender stereotypes are learned, often from media (ads, films, songs, toys), and can be spotted and questioned
Roles, jobs, traits, colours and feelings are not owned by one gender; counter-examples are everywhere
Media-literacy plus 'flip it' practice (rewriting a stereotyped message to a fair one) builds the habit of challenging bias

scenarios.hook: An ad for a cleaning product. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: A smiling mum scrubs the floor while the family relaxes
The voice says "every mother wants a clean home"

scenarios.why: Ads often show only women doing the cleaning, as if it's only their job.
scenarios.relearn: Cleaning ads often stereotype housework as only women's work; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A toy advert. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: Boys play with cars and building sets
Girls play with dolls and kitchen sets

scenarios.why: Toy ads often split toys by gender, even though any kid can enjoy any toy.
scenarios.relearn: Toy ads stereotype toys as 'for boys' or 'for girls'; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A film scene. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: The girl waits to be rescued
The boy does the brave rescue

scenarios.why: Films often make girls helpless and boys the heroes; real life isn't like that.
scenarios.relearn: Films often stereotype girls as helpless and boys as heroes; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A school textbook picture. Spot the stereotype.
scenarios.why: Books often show men as doctors and women as nurses, but both can be either.
scenarios.relearn: Books often stereotype men as doctors, women as nurses; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A fairness-cream ad. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: A girl only gets the job after her skin turns fairer

scenarios.why: These ads push the false idea that fairer skin means more worth or success.
scenarios.relearn: Fairness-cream ads stereotype fair skin as better; that's false.

scenarios.hook: A cricket broadcast. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: The commentator ignores the women's match entirely

scenarios.why: Sport coverage often treats men's games as the 'real' ones and sidelines women's.
scenarios.relearn: Sport media often stereotypes men's sport as the only 'real' sport; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A song lyric. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: "Boys will be boys" as an excuse for bad behaviour

scenarios.why: Some lyrics excuse boys and silence girls; those are stereotypes, not rules.
scenarios.relearn: 'Boys will be boys' and 'good girls stay quiet' are stereotypes, not truths.

scenarios.hook: A greeting card. Spot the stereotype.
scenarios.why: Even cards box kids in: boys = strong, girls = pretty. Kids are all of these.
scenarios.relearn: Cards often stereotype boys as 'strong' and girls as 'pretty'; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A cooking-show line-up. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: The famous TV chef is a man
"Cooking at home is a woman's duty"

scenarios.why: Funny twist: top chefs are often men, yet home cooking is called 'women's work'.
scenarios.relearn: Cooking isn't gendered; the 'home cooking is women's duty' line is a stereotype.

scenarios.hook: A car advert. Spot the stereotype.

scene.text: A man drives the powerful car

scenarios.why: Car ads often make men the drivers and women the decoration.
scenarios.relearn: Car ads often stereotype men as drivers and women as decoration; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A 'family' emoji set. Spot the stereotype.
scenarios.why: Even emojis can assume mums care and dads earn; both parents can do both.
scenarios.relearn: Defaults often stereotype mums as carers and dads as earners; spot it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: once you start spotting stereotypes in media, you see them everywhere. Noticing more?
scenarios.affirm: That radar is media literacy, and it's a superpower.
scenarios.relearn: Spotting stereotypes in media is a skill that grows with practice.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a stereotype is a too-simple story about a whole group. Make sense?
scenarios.affirm: Real people are far richer than any stereotype.
scenarios.relearn: A stereotype is an over-simple story about a whole group.

scenarios.hook: "If I see it on TV, it must be how things really are."

myth.un: What media shows is how the world really is.
myth.re: Media is made by people and often repeats stereotypes.
myth.why: Screens show choices made by writers, not simple truth.

scenarios.relearn: Media isn't reality; it often repeats stereotypes.

scenarios.hook: "Stereotypes are harmless, just a bit of fun."

myth.un: Gender stereotypes are harmless fun.
myth.re: They quietly limit what kids think they're allowed to be.
myth.why: Repeated messages shape what feels 'normal'.

scenarios.relearn: Stereotypes aren't harmless; they limit what people feel free to be.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a stereotype, or just a fact?
scenarios.relearn: Stereotypes about what a gender 'can' do aren't facts.

scenarios.hook: Sort these jobs: who can do them?
scenarios.relearn: Every job can be done by anyone, whatever their gender.

scenarios.hook: "Flying planes is a man's job."

myth.un: Flying planes is a man's job.
myth.re: Women fly planes too; India has one of the world's highest shares of women pilots.
myth.why: Skill, not gender, decides who can fly.

scenarios.relearn: Women are pilots too; flying isn't a 'man's job'.

scenarios.hook: "Cooking is for women; men can't cook."

myth.un: Cooking is women's work; men can't cook.
myth.re: Anyone can cook; many top chefs are men, and dads cook too.
myth.why: Cooking is a skill, not a gender.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone can cook; it isn't 'women's work'.

scenarios.hook: Match the role to a real person who breaks the stereotype.
scenarios.relearn: Real people break gender stereotypes in every field.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a chore, and who 'should' do it?
scenarios.relearn: All home chores can be shared by anyone, not split by gender.

scenarios.hook: Your group is picking a class captain; someone says "it should be a boy".

options.text: Say "anyone can lead; let's pick the best person"
options.consequence: The choice opens up fairly.

options.text: Go along with 'a boy'
options.consequence: Leadership isn't gendered; the best person can be anyone.

scenarios.debrief: Leadership isn't a boy or girl thing, it's a skill thing.
scenarios.relearn: Anyone can be a leader, regardless of gender.

scenarios.hook: "Nursing is only for women."

myth.un: Only women can be nurses.
myth.re: Men are nurses too; caring is a skill anyone can have.
myth.why: Care work isn't owned by one gender.

scenarios.relearn: Men can be nurses; caring isn't only for women.

scenarios.hook: "Girls aren't good at science and maths."

myth.un: Girls aren't good at science or maths.
myth.re: Girls do brilliantly in science and maths everywhere.
myth.why: Ability isn't decided by gender.

scenarios.relearn: Girls excel in science and maths; the stereotype is false.

scenarios.hook: A friend says "boys shouldn't do dance class".

options.text: Point out famous male dancers and that anyone can dance
options.consequence: Your friend rethinks it.

options.text: Agree to avoid teasing
options.consequence: Dance is for anyone; many celebrated dancers are men.

scenarios.debrief: Dance, like any art, is open to everyone.
scenarios.relearn: Boys can dance; the arts aren't gendered.

scenarios.hook: Match the job to the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Jobs and family roles aren't limited by gender.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: name a job you'd love, does your gender stop you? (It doesn't.)
scenarios.affirm: Your dreams aren't limited by your gender, ever.
scenarios.relearn: Your gender doesn't limit the job you can dream of.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when a home shares all chores, everyone wins. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Shared chores mean a fairer, happier home.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing chores fairly helps everyone at home.

scenarios.hook: "Driving is a man's thing."

myth.un: Driving is really a man's thing.
myth.re: Women drive everything from scooters to planes to trucks.
myth.why: Driving is a skill, not a gender.

scenarios.relearn: Driving isn't a 'man's thing'; anyone can drive.

scenarios.hook: Sort: breaks a job stereotype, or repeats one?
scenarios.relearn: Breaking job stereotypes shows what's really possible.

scenarios.hook: "Boys don't cry."

myth.un: Real boys don't cry.
myth.re: Everyone cries; it's healthy, not weak.
myth.why: Feelings aren't a gender; bottling them up hurts.

scenarios.relearn: Boys cry too; feelings aren't weakness.

scenarios.hook: "Be a man, toughen up, don't feel things."

myth.un: Being a man means never showing feelings.
myth.re: Strong people feel and express emotions.
myth.why: Hiding all feelings isn't strength, it's strain.

scenarios.relearn: Real strength includes feeling and showing emotions.

scenarios.hook: "You throw like a girl" (as an insult).

myth.un: 'Like a girl' means weak or bad.
myth.re: 'Like a girl' can mean strong, fast and skilled.
myth.why: Using a gender as an insult is the stereotype.

scenarios.relearn: 'Like a girl' isn't an insult; girls are strong and skilled.

scenarios.hook: "Girls are too emotional to lead."

myth.un: Girls are too emotional to be good leaders.
myth.re: Understanding emotions makes someone a better leader.
myth.why: Emotional skill is a leadership strength.

scenarios.relearn: Being in touch with emotions helps leadership; it doesn't block it.

scenarios.hook: "Girls can't be angry; they should be sweet."

myth.un: Girls should always be sweet, never angry.
myth.re: Everyone feels anger; girls are allowed to as well.
myth.why: Demanding only 'sweet' silences real feelings.

scenarios.relearn: Girls can feel and show anger like anyone else.

scenarios.hook: "Boys must always be brave and never scared."

myth.un: Boys must always be brave and never afraid.
myth.re: Everyone feels fear; admitting it is brave too.
myth.why: Pretending you're never scared is its own pressure.

scenarios.relearn: Boys feel fear too; admitting it is okay and brave.

scenarios.hook: "Caring and gentleness are only for girls."

myth.un: Being caring and gentle is only for girls.
myth.re: Kindness and gentleness suit everyone.
myth.why: Good qualities aren't owned by a gender.

scenarios.relearn: Caring and gentleness are for everyone, not just girls.

scenarios.hook: A boy in your class is crying and others start mocking him.

options.text: Say "it's okay to cry" and stand with him
options.consequence: You ease the shame; others may stop.

options.text: Join the mocking so you're not next
options.consequence: Crying isn't shameful; standing with him is the kinder, braver move.

scenarios.debrief: Mocking a boy for crying enforces a harmful stereotype.
scenarios.relearn: Support someone showing feelings; don't shame them.

scenarios.hook: A girl wants to try out for the football team; people laugh.

options.text: Encourage her and cheer her on
options.consequence: She tries out; maybe others follow.

options.text: Laugh along
options.consequence: Girls play football brilliantly; back her up.

scenarios.debrief: Sport is for every gender; back people who break the mould.
scenarios.relearn: Girls can play any sport; cheer them on.

scenarios.hook: Your friend says "asking for help is for girls; men sort it alone".

options.text: Say "asking for help is smart for anyone"
options.consequence: You reframe help as strength.

options.text: Agree and never ask for help
options.consequence: Asking for help is a strength, not a gender thing.

scenarios.debrief: 'Tough it out alone' is a harmful stereotype, help-seeking is healthy.
scenarios.relearn: Asking for help is smart for everyone, regardless of gender.

scenarios.hook: Someone tells you "man up, stop whining".
scenarios.relearn: You can push back on 'man up'; feelings are human.

scenarios.hook: A friend mocks another girl for being 'bossy' when she leads.
scenarios.relearn: A girl who leads is a leader, not 'bossy'.

scenarios.hook: Someone says "that colour/hobby is too girly for you".
scenarios.relearn: You can like what you like; tastes aren't gendered.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which feeling are you sometimes told to hide because of your gender?
scenarios.affirm: All your feelings are allowed; none belong to one gender.
scenarios.relearn: No feeling is off-limits because of your gender.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'strong' can mean lifting weights or sharing how you feel. Both count?
scenarios.affirm: Emotional strength counts just as much as physical strength.
scenarios.relearn: Strength includes emotional openness, not just muscle.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a world where boys can cry and girls can lead, better for everyone?
scenarios.affirm: Dropping these rules frees everyone to be fully themselves.
scenarios.relearn: Letting go of gender rules frees everyone.

scenarios.hook: "Pink is for girls, blue is for boys."

myth.un: Pink is for girls and blue is for boys.
myth.re: Colours are for everyone; pink was once a 'boy' colour.
myth.why: Colour rules are made up and they change.

scenarios.relearn: Colours have no gender; anyone can like any colour.

scenarios.hook: "Boys can't have long hair."

myth.un: Boys shouldn't have long hair.
myth.re: Hair length is a personal choice, not a gender rule.
myth.why: Across history and cultures, all genders wore long hair.

scenarios.relearn: Hair length is personal, not a gender rule.

scenarios.hook: "Girls must wear dresses; trousers aren't for them."

myth.un: Girls should only wear dresses.
myth.re: Girls wear whatever is comfortable, trousers included.
myth.why: Clothes are about comfort and choice, not rules.

scenarios.relearn: Girls can wear trousers or anything; clothes aren't gendered.

scenarios.hook: "Dolls are for girls; boys shouldn't play with them."

myth.un: Dolls are only for girls.
myth.re: Playing with dolls helps any kid practise caring.
myth.why: Toys teach skills, not gender.

scenarios.relearn: Any child can play with dolls; toys aren't gendered.

scenarios.hook: Sort: who is this colour/toy/clothing for?
scenarios.relearn: Colours, toys and clothes are for anyone who likes them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a made-up rule, or a real reason?
scenarios.relearn: Gendered looks 'rules' are made up; safety and hygiene rules are real.

scenarios.hook: Sort: colour facts.

items.text: Pink was once seen as a strong 'boy' colour
Colours have feelings of their own
Liking blue makes you a boy

scenarios.relearn: Colour-gender links are invented and have changed over time.

scenarios.hook: A shop's kids section. Spot the stereotype.
scenarios.why: Splitting shops into pink-girl and blue-boy aisles is a made-up divide.
scenarios.relearn: Shops often stereotype with pink-girl, blue-boy aisles; spot it.

scenarios.hook: A birthday party theme list. Spot the stereotype.
scenarios.why: Party themes get split by gender, but any kid can love any theme.
scenarios.relearn: Party themes aren't gendered; spot the split.

scenarios.hook: Match the item to the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Everyday items aren't owned by one gender.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: wear and like what you enjoy, who does that hurt? (No one.)
scenarios.affirm: Your tastes are yours; enjoying them harms no one.
scenarios.relearn: Liking what you like harms no one; it's your choice.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: imagine if no toy or colour had a gender label. Freeing?
scenarios.affirm: Without labels, you're free to enjoy it all.
scenarios.relearn: Dropping gender labels on stuff frees everyone's choices.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Girls are bad at sports."

myth.un: Girls are bad at sports.
myth.re: Girls are champions in every sport.
myth.why: Skill comes from practice, not gender.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'girls are bad at sports' to 'girls are champions'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Boys can't take care of babies."

myth.un: Boys can't take care of babies.
myth.re: Boys and men make caring, capable parents.
myth.why: Caring is learned, not gendered.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'boys can't care for babies' to 'men are caring parents'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Leaders are men."

myth.un: Leaders are men.
myth.re: Leaders are people of any gender with vision and care.
myth.why: Leadership is a skill set, not a gender.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'leaders are men' to 'leaders can be anyone'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Girls should stay home."

myth.un: A girl's place is at home.
myth.re: Girls belong anywhere they choose, school, work, the world.
myth.why: No place is off-limits because of gender.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'girls stay home' to 'girls belong anywhere they choose'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Real men don't do housework."

myth.un: Real men don't do housework.
myth.re: Sharing housework is exactly what fair, real partners do.
myth.why: A home runs on everyone pitching in.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'men don't do housework' to 'fair partners share it'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Boys are naturally smarter."

myth.un: Boys are naturally smarter than girls.
myth.re: Intelligence isn't decided by gender at all.
myth.why: Brains don't come in 'boy' or 'girl' versions.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'boys are smarter' to 'intelligence isn't gendered'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Pretty is the most important thing for a girl."

myth.un: Being pretty is the most important thing for a girl.
myth.re: Girls matter for their minds, skills and kindness, not just looks.
myth.why: Worth isn't a beauty score.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'pretty matters most' to 'her mind and skills matter most'.

scenarios.hook: Flip it: "Boys who like reading or art are weird."

myth.un: Boys who like reading or art are weird.
myth.re: Boys who love books and art are just being themselves.
myth.why: Interests don't have a gender.

scenarios.relearn: Flip 'art is weird for boys' to 'any interest fits any kid'.

scenarios.hook: You're remixing an old advert for class. It shows only mum cooking.

options.text: Remix it: show the whole family cooking together
options.consequence: Your flipped ad models fairness.

options.text: Leave it as is
options.consequence: Flipping it to a shared scene challenges the stereotype.

scenarios.debrief: Remaking a stereotyped message into a fair one is 'flipping the script'.
scenarios.relearn: You can remix stereotyped media into fair messages.

scenarios.hook: You're writing a story; the default hero is a boy who rescues a girl.

options.text: Flip it: make either character the hero, or both
options.consequence: Your story breaks the tired mould.

options.text: Keep the default
options.consequence: Flipping the roles makes a fresher, fairer story.

scenarios.debrief: Stories don't have to follow the old gender script.
scenarios.relearn: You can write heroes of any gender.

scenarios.hook: A friend says "that's a girls' game, you can't play".

yourLine.text: "Games don't have a gender, deal me in."

scenarios.relearn: You can flip 'that's a girls'/boys' game' on the spot.

scenarios.hook: Someone says "you can't be a doctor, you're a girl".

yourLine.text: "Watch me, girls are doctors all the time."

scenarios.relearn: You can flip 'a girl can't be a doctor' with confidence.

scenarios.hook: You're checking your own remix for hidden stereotypes. Spot any.

scene.text: The boss character is still always a man
The team is mixed and fair
The carer is still always a woman

scenarios.why: Even when flipping, old defaults can sneak back; check your own work.
scenarios.relearn: Check even your own work for stereotypes that sneak in.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: flipping a stereotype out loud, does it get easier with practice?
scenarios.affirm: Flipping scripts is a muscle, it strengthens every time.
scenarios.relearn: Challenging stereotypes gets easier the more you practise.

scenarios.hook: An elder says "girls shouldn't laugh so loudly".

yourLine.text: "I think everyone should be free to laugh, na?"

scenarios.relearn: You can question a stereotype respectfully, even with elders.

scenarios.hook: A classmate says "ew, that's so gay" about a boy liking pink.

yourLine.text: "Liking a colour is just liking a colour, leave him be."

scenarios.relearn: You can call out put-downs that police how others express themselves.

scenarios.hook: A relative says to your brother "you're the man, you'll handle money; she'll cook".

yourLine.text: "We can both learn money and cooking, right?"

scenarios.relearn: You can gently offer a fairer view when roles get assigned by gender.

scenarios.hook: Friends chant "boys are better" at a match.
scenarios.relearn: You can refuse and reframe 'one gender is better' chants.

scenarios.hook: A teacher only ever picks boys to carry heavy things and girls to decorate.

options.text: Politely ask if everyone can get a turn at both
options.consequence: The teacher rethinks the split.

options.text: Say nothing
options.consequence: A polite question can open up fairer choices.

scenarios.debrief: Even well-meant habits can stereotype; a kind question helps.
scenarios.relearn: You can ask, kindly, for tasks to be shared beyond gender.

scenarios.hook: Online, a video mocks boys who do ballet. Friends are sharing it.

options.text: Don't share; comment that ballet takes huge strength
options.consequence: You break the pile-on with a fact.

options.text: Share it for the laughs
options.consequence: Ballet is athletic and tough; don't amplify the mockery.

scenarios.debrief: You can refuse to spread stereotype-mocking content.
scenarios.relearn: Don't amplify content that mocks people for breaking gender norms.

scenarios.hook: Your little cousin is told "don't be a sissy". You're nearby.

options.text: Reassure them: "feeling scared is normal and okay"
options.consequence: You undo a little of the harm.

options.text: Ignore it
options.consequence: A kind word counters the 'sissy' shaming.

scenarios.debrief: You can be the voice that flips a harmful message for a younger kid.
scenarios.relearn: You can reassure a younger child against gender shaming.

scenarios.hook: "Calling out a stereotype is rude or 'too much'."

myth.un: Pointing out a stereotype is rude or too much.
myth.re: Questioning unfairness, kindly, is fair and brave.
myth.why: Politeness and standing up can go together.

scenarios.relearn: Calling out a stereotype kindly is brave, not rude.

scenarios.hook: "One person can't change how people think."

myth.un: One kid speaking up changes nothing.
myth.re: One voice often gives others courage to agree.
myth.why: Change usually starts with one person.

scenarios.relearn: One voice flipping a stereotype can spark others.

scenarios.hook: "It's not my problem if a stereotype isn't about me."

myth.un: Stereotypes that don't target me aren't my problem.
myth.re: Speaking up for others is how fairness spreads.
myth.why: Allies make the biggest difference.

scenarios.relearn: You can speak up against stereotypes even when they're not about you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what's your go-to line for flipping a stereotype now?
scenarios.affirm: Keep that line ready, you're now a script-flipper.
scenarios.relearn: Having a ready line helps you flip stereotypes in the moment.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: biggest take-away from Flip the Script?
scenarios.affirm: Spot it, flip it, call it out, you've got the whole move.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the stereotype, flip it, and call it out, that's the skill.
